## Exercise 6: start from generic MLIR {#arithmetic-objective}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```bash
cat examples/ex6_arith_muli.mlir
```

<div class="code-gap"></div>

```mlir
module {
  func.func @ex6_mul(%a : i8, %b : i8) -> i8 {
    %r = arith.muli %a, %b : i8
    return %r : i8
  }
}
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
**Objective: a combinational hardware module**

```mlir
hw.module @ex6_mul(
    in %in0 : i8, in %in1 : i8, out out0 : i8) {
  %0 = comb.mul %in0, %in1 : i8
  hw.output %0 : i8
}
```

This is the smallest complete path to SystemVerilog and logic synthesis.
:::
:::
::::

## Exercise 6: find the missing passes - 3 min {#arithmetic-exercise-6}

To reach that objective, two things must change:

- `func.func` and `return` must become a hardware module boundary.
- `arith.muli` must become a combinational multiplier.

Does upstream `circt-opt` provide both transformations?

```bash
circt-opt --help | grep -i arith
circt-opt --help | grep -i func
```

:::: {.columns .fragment}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Relevant `arith` result**

```text
--convert-comb-to-arith
--lower-hwarith-to-hw
--map-arith-to-comb
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Relevant `func` result**

```text
--lower-cf-to-handshake
    Lower func and CF into Handshake IR
```

No direct generic `func.func` → `hw.module` pass.
:::
::::

Run the same two-stage pipeline on `examples/ex6_arith_mulf.mlir`:

## `map-arith-to-comb` draws a deliberate line {#arithmetic-map-contract}

```{.text code-line-numbers="2,4|5-6|9-13"}
def MapArithToCombPass : Pass<"map-arith-to-comb"> {
  let summary = "Map arith ops to combinational logic";
  let description = [{
    A pass which does a simple `arith` to `comb` mapping wherever possible.
    This pass will not convert:
    * floating point operations
    * operations using `vector`-typed values

    This does not intend to be the definitive lowering/HLS pass of `arith`
    operations in CIRCT (hence the name "map" instead of e.g. "lower").
    Rather, it provides a simple way (mostly for testing purposes) to map
    `arith` operations.
  }];
}
```

[CIRCT `Transforms/Passes.td`, pinned `firtool-1.147.0` source](https://github.com/llvm/circt/blob/firtool-1.147.0/include/circt/Transforms/Passes.td#L56-L76)

The failure is the documented boundary of the pass. Our exercise supplies one
concrete floating-point lowering.

## Eight bits encode several numerical regimes {#arithmetic-e4m3-format}

::: {.bit-layout}
::: {.bit-field .sign}
**s**

`[7]`

<small>sign · 1 bit</small>
:::
::: {.bit-field .exponent}
**eeee**

`[6:3]`

<small>biased exponent · 4 bits</small>
:::
::: {.bit-field .fraction}
**mmm**

`[2:0]`

<small>stored fraction · 3 bits</small>
:::
:::

| Regime | Encoding | Value |
|---|---|---|
| zero | `e = 0000`, `m = 000` | $0$ |
| subnormal | `e = 0000`, `m != 000` | $(-1)^s 2^{-6}(m/8)$ |
| normal | `e != 0000` | $(-1)^s 2^{e-7}(1+m/8)$ |
| NaN | `e = 1111`, `m = 111` | not a number |

`f8E4M3FN` has bias 7, finite values up to 448, and no infinity.
[@micikevicius2022fp8]

## Subnormals fill the gap around zero {#arithmetic-e4m3-axis}

![](assets/images/e4m3-number-line.svg){fig-alt="Positive E4M3FN values near zero, with subnormal and normal ranges distinguished" width="100%"}

| Bits | Hex | Value |
|---|---:|---:|
| `0 0000 001` | `0x01` | $2^{-9}$ = 0.001953125 |
| `0 0000 111` | `0x07` | $7 \times 2^{-9}$ = 0.013671875 |
| `0 0001 000` | `0x08` | $2^{-6}$ = 0.015625 |

The sign bit mirrors these points onto the negative axis.

## The same format spans tiny values to 448 {#arithmetic-e4m3-values}

| Hex | Fields `s eeee mmm` | Value |
|---:|---|---:|
| `0x00` | `0 0000 000` | 0 |
| `0x08` | `0 0001 000` | $2^{-6}$ |
| `0x30` | `0 0110 000` | 0.5 |
| `0x38` | `0 0111 000` | 1 |
| `0x3C` | `0 0111 100` | 1.5 |
| `0x41` | `0 1000 001` | 2.25 |
| `0x7E` | `0 1111 110` | 448 |
| `0x7F` | `0 1111 111` | NaN |

Less precision buys a smaller representation and more operations per watt;
the exact rounding and exceptional-value rules remain part of the contract.

## Exercise 7: first draw the datapath {#arithmetic-pass-goal}

::: {.e4m3-objective-source}
```mlir
%r = arith.mulf %a, %b : f8E4M3FN
```
:::

::: {.e4m3-objective-line}
The operation states **what** to compute. In hardware, we first choose **how the data will flow**.
:::

::: {.e4m3-datapath-frame .e4m3-objective-schematic}
![](assets/images/digital-design/e4m3-normal-multiplier.svg#objective){.e4m3-datapath fig-alt="Normal-path E4M3 multiplier datapath"}
:::

::: {.e4m3-figure-caption}
Normal-path E4M3 multiplier, adapted from [@ledoux2024thesis, Fig. 3.9].
:::

::: {.e4m3-scope-line}
**First checkpoint:** normal, finite, non-zero operands; normal result; no rounding yet.
:::

## Checkpoint 1: materialize the hidden one {#arithmetic-hidden-one}

::: {.e4m3-build-layout}
::: {.e4m3-datapath-frame}
![](assets/images/digital-design/e4m3-normal-multiplier.svg#hidden){.e4m3-datapath fig-alt="E4M3 multiplier with the hidden-one stage highlighted"}
:::

::: {.e4m3-step-copy}
For a normal E4M3 number, the stored field `mmm` represents the significand
$1.mmm_2$. The leading `1` is implicit in memory but must become a wire.

```mlir
%fa = comb.extract %a from 0 : (i8) -> i3
%fb = comb.extract %b from 0 : (i8) -> i3
%one = hw.constant 1 : i1
%ma4 = comb.concat %one, %fa : i1, i3
%mb4 = comb.concat %one, %fb : i1, i3
```

`0x3C` stores `100`, so its effective significand is `1.100₂ = 1.5`.
:::
:::

## Exercise 7A: preserve the full product - 5 min {#arithmetic-exercise-7a}

::: {.e4m3-build-layout}
::: {.e4m3-datapath-frame}
![](assets/images/digital-design/e4m3-normal-multiplier.svg#multiply-view){.e4m3-datapath fig-alt="E4M3 multiplier with the significand multiplication stage highlighted"}
:::

::: {.e4m3-step-copy}
`comb.mul` produces the same width as its operands. A four-by-four-bit
significand multiplication needs **eight result bits**.

Complete the zero extension and produce `%raw : i8` in
`buildE4M3FNMultiplier`.

::: {.fragment}
```mlir
%zero4 = hw.constant 0 : i4
%ma8 = comb.concat %zero4, %ma4 : i4, i4
%mb8 = comb.concat %zero4, %mb4 : i4, i4
%raw = comb.mul %ma8, %mb8 : i8
```
:::
:::
:::

## Checkpoint 2: one bit selects the normalization {#arithmetic-normalization-bit}

::: {.e4m3-build-layout}
::: {.e4m3-datapath-frame}
![](assets/images/digital-design/e4m3-normal-multiplier.svg#normalize-view){.e4m3-datapath fig-alt="E4M3 multiplier with the normalization and exponent-adjust stages highlighted"}
:::

::: {.e4m3-step-copy}
Normal significands are in $[1,2)$, so their product is in $[1,4)$.

::: {.e4m3-normal-table}
| `%raw[7]` | Normalized significand | Exponent |
|---:|---|---:|
| `0` | use `%raw[6:3]` | `+ 0` |
| `1` | use `%raw[7:4]` | `+ 1` |
:::

::: {.e4m3-equation}
`1.100₂ × 1.100₂ = 10.010000₂`
:::

For `0x3C × 0x3C`, the leading bit lands in `%raw[7]`: shift once and
increment the exponent to obtain `0x41` ($2.25$).
:::
:::

## Exercise 7B: one bit controls two paths - 7 min {#arithmetic-exercise-7b}

::: {.e4m3-build-layout}
::: {.e4m3-datapath-frame}
![](assets/images/digital-design/e4m3-normal-multiplier.svg#normalize-view){.e4m3-datapath fig-alt="E4M3 multiplier with the normalization and exponent-adjust stages highlighted"}
:::

::: {.e4m3-step-copy}
Use `%norm = %raw[7]` to select the four normalized significand bits and to
increment the exponent path.

::: {.fragment}
```mlir
%norm = comb.extract %raw from 7 : (i8) -> i1
%direct = comb.extract %raw from 3 : (i8) -> i4
%shifted = comb.extract %raw from 4 : (i8) -> i4
%mant = comb.mux %norm, %shifted, %direct : i4
%norm5 = comb.concat %zero4, %norm : i4, i1
%adjusted = comb.add %base, %norm5 : i5
```
:::
:::
:::

## Complete the first normal-path circuit {#arithmetic-normal-path}

::: {.e4m3-build-layout}
::: {.e4m3-datapath-frame}
![](assets/images/digital-design/e4m3-normal-multiplier.svg#complete){.e4m3-datapath fig-alt="Completed normal-path E4M3 multiplier with the result packing highlighted"}
:::

::: {.e4m3-step-copy}
The remaining sign, exponent, and packing logic is supplied with the first
solution checkpoint.

```mlir
%sign = comb.xor %sa, %sb : i1
%sum = comb.add %ea5, %eb5 : i5
%bias = hw.constant 7 : i5
%base = comb.sub %sum, %bias : i5

%frac = comb.extract %mant from 0 : (i4) -> i3
%exp = comb.extract %adjusted from 0 : (i5) -> i4
%result = comb.concat %sign, %exp, %frac : i1, i4, i3
```

The custom pass owns `f8E4M3FN → i8`; `--tutorial-func-to-hw` only converts
the function boundary afterward.
:::
:::

## This checkpoint is intentionally incomplete {#arithmetic-special-cases}

| Excluded case | Hardware still required |
|---|---|
| discarded product bits | round to nearest, ties to even |
| zero or subnormal input | the hidden bit is not always `1` |
| subnormal result | gradual-underflow shift and rounding |
| exponent overflow | E4M3FN overflow behavior |
| NaN input | detect and return the NaN encoding |

The normal-path circuit should compile, but the exhaustive checker is expected
to expose these missing cases:

```bash
./scripts/test-e4m3-all.py --pass
```

The complete reference is `examples/ex7_e4m3fn_mul_reference.sv`.

## If time: specialize a squarer {#arithmetic-square-extension}

`examples/optional_e4m3fn_square.mlir` contains `%x * %x`.

- Match equal SSA operands.
- Decode `%x` once.
- Emit a dedicated significand squarer.
- Prove equivalence, then compare AIG nodes and depth.
